title: 1 Kings 18:1–16
context: In the third year the LORD sends Elijah to show himself to Ahab and promises rain. Ahab and his household steward Obadiah, who feared the LORD and had hidden one hundred prophets from Jezebel’s purge, divide the land to search for grass, and Elijah meets Obadiah on the way. Obadiah fears that Elijah will vanish and Ahab will kill him, but Elijah swears he will appear to Ahab that day. The New Testament speaks of three years and six months without rain (Luke 4:25; James 5:17), and interpreters reconcile this with the third year here in different ways, for example by counting from different starting points. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about quiet faithfulness under a hostile ruler, the cost of serving God in a compromised setting, and the LORD keeping his word to send rain.

verses.text: After many days, the LORD’s word came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, “Go, show yourself to Ahab; and I will send rain on the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Elijah in the third year, sending him to Ahab with the promise of rain. Judgment is not God’s final word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD determining both the drought and its end. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s mercy after discipline.

verses.text: Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah going to show himself to Ahab while the famine is severe in Samaria. Obedience takes him into danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the severity of the famine as the backdrop for God’s coming display of power. Both traditions commonly read the verse as courage grounded in God’s command.

verses.text: Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah, who was over Ahab’s household, introduced as one who feared the LORD greatly. Faithfulness can exist in unlikely places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Obadiah as one of God’s faithful people preserved within a corrupt court. Readers in both traditions commonly honor his reverence for the LORD.

verses.text: for when Jezebel cut off the LORD’s prophets, Obadiah took one hundred prophets, and hid them fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water.)
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah hiding one hundred prophets in caves and feeding them while Jezebel killed the LORD’s prophets. His courage is quiet but costly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God preserving his servants through Obadiah’s actions. Both traditions commonly hold up this verse as an example of faith working through practical protection of the vulnerable.

verses.text: Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land, to all the springs of water, and to all the brooks. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, that we not lose all the animals.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ahab concerned to find grass to save the horses and mules. His focus is on the animals rather than repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ahab’s practical concern as revealing his spiritual blindness during judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly note the contrast between his worry and his refusal to turn to the LORD.

verses.text: So they divided the land between them to pass throughout it. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went another way by himself.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ahab and Obadiah dividing the land to search for water and grass. The king and his servant go separate ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the separation as setting up Obadiah’s meeting with Elijah by God’s providence. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple narrative step.

verses.text: As Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. He recognized him, and fell on his face, and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah meeting Elijah and falling on his face in recognition. He shows respect to the LORD’s prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting as arranged by God. Readers in both traditions commonly read Obadiah’s posture as reverence for the prophet who speaks the LORD’s word.

verses.text: He answered him, “It is I. Go, tell your lord, ‘Behold, Elijah is here!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah telling Obadiah to announce his presence to Ahab. The prophet makes his return public after years in hiding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s command as a step in God’s plan for the confrontation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the beginning of open engagement with Ahab.

verses.text: He said, “How have I sinned, that you would deliver your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah fearing that the message will lead Ahab to kill him. His fear is understandable given the danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Obadiah’s question as honest anxiety in a perilous role. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy for his position.

verses.text: As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he took an oath of the kingdom and nation that they didn’t find you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah describing how Ahab searched every nation and kingdom for Elijah. The king’s determination is intense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the search as showing how God hid his prophet despite the king’s efforts. Both traditions commonly read the verse as highlighting God’s protection.

verses.text: Now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Behold, Elijah is here.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah repeating Elijah’s instruction with alarm. The command feels far too dangerous to carry out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his repetition as emphasizing the risk he faces. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as heightening the tension before the confrontation.

verses.text: It will happen, as soon as I leave you, that the LORD’s Spirit will carry you I don’t know where; and so when I come and tell Ahab, and he can’t find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared the LORD from my youth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah fearing that the LORD’s Spirit will carry Elijah away, leaving him to face Ahab alone. He reminds Elijah that he has feared the LORD from his youth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his concern as reflecting Elijah’s unpredictable movements under the Spirit’s guidance. Both traditions commonly honor Obadiah’s lifelong reverence.

verses.text: Wasn’t it told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the LORD’s prophets, how I hid one hundred men of the LORD’s prophets with fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah reminding Elijah that he hid one hundred prophets. He appeals to his proven faithfulness in a dangerous season.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reminder as evidence of God’s preserving grace in a dark time. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a defense of his loyalty.

verses.text: Now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Behold, Elijah is here”.’ He will kill me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah repeating his fear that Ahab will kill him. He needs assurance from the prophet before he acts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as showing the weight of the danger. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an honest expression of fear that God answers through Elijah’s oath.

verses.text: Elijah said, “As the LORD of Armies lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah swearing by the LORD of Armies that he will show himself to Ahab that day. His oath gives Obadiah confidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as grounded in Elijah’s service before the living God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as firm assurance.

verses.text: So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him; and Ahab went to meet Elijah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Obadiah going to tell Ahab, and Ahab going to meet Elijah. The stage is set for open confrontation on Carmel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting as the result of God’s guiding hand. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a narrative transition to the contest.
